US securities regulators are investigating the accounting practices of Nvidia, according to US media, adding to the turmoil engulfing the artificial intelligence chip giant following the resignation of its chief executive. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) inquiry is in its early stages, The New York Times reported Saturday, citing people briefed on the confidential investigation. The Wall Street Journal reported on the investigation earlier this week, although it was unable to establish its precise focus. The probe could end without any charges being brought against the company. Questions about Nvidia's financial disclosures have intensified amid scrutiny of its dealings with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company investigated by American authorities over suspected shipments of restricted AI chips to China. Nvidia last year changed how it reported sales by geographical location, switching from customers' billing addresses to the countries where they are headquartered, US media reported. The change removed Singapore from its geographical breakdown, despite the company's significant business there. It remains unclear whether the SEC investigation is connected to those accounting changes or to the scandal surrounding former chief executive Jensen Huang. Huang resigned earlier this month following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive suspected by US intelligence of working for Beijing. China has denied the espionage allegations, while Megaspeed has maintained that it operates lawfully. Nvidia's board has appointed former chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO and launched an investigation into the circumstances surrounding Huang's departure. The upheaval has shaken investor confidence in one of the world's most valuable companies, whose advanced semiconductors have been central to the global AI boom. Nvidia shares plunged 14 percent on Friday, bringing their losses for the week to more than 20 percent. US President Donald Trump nevertheless called Friday for Huang to be reinstated. "I think that I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance," Trump told reporters. But Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones has ruled out his return, saying board directors unanimously accepted his resignation. Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results

On Nov. 12, Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) founder and chief executive officer Jensen Huang resigned from his post after a series of extramarital affairs (including one with an alleged Chinese spy) came to light. To make matters worse, the U.S. government is now investigating some of the company's customers in Southeast Asia to determine whether advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips were illegally forwarded to businesses in China. Nvidia stock has plummeted by 37% from its peak amid the turmoil, and it's now trading at the cheapest valuation in a decade. However, the company just reported a blockbuster set of operating results for its fiscal 2027 third quarter (ended Oct. 25), and interim CEO Colette Kress even issued a higher revenue forecast for the upcoming 2028 fiscal year. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » As a result, while Nvidia's challenges are likely to cause further short-term volatility in its stock, I think its booming business and solid fundamentals will ultimately prevail. Here's where I predict the stock will be trading in one year. Nvidia has come a long way since launching its first dedicated AI graphics processing unit (GPU) for the data center, the Hopper-based H100, in 2022. It went on to release the Blackwell and Blackwell Ultra architectures in 2024 and 2025, the latter of which can deliver up to 50 times more output performance than Hopper. But Nvidia started shipping its new Vera Rubin systems during the recent third quarter, which include the Rubin GPU, Vera central processing unit (CPU), and a series of upgraded networking components. It can deliver up to 30 times the performance of the equivalent Blackwell Ultra system, translating into a potential 97% reduction in inference token costs. Inference tokens are the text, images, or computer code generated by an AI model in response to a prompt, so Vera Rubin could significantly reduce the cost of running AI software. This is likely to drive greater AI adoption while making data center operators more profitable, fueling further demand for Nvidia's chips. Colette Kress said Vera Rubin achieved almost $20 billion in sales during the third quarter alone, making this the fastest product ramp in Nvidia's history. Nvidia generated a record $115.8 billion in revenue during the third quarter, a whopping 103% increase from the year-ago period. The data center segment alone accounted for $107.6 billion of that total, and it grew at an even faster pace of 110%. Nvidia's physical AI business also deserves a mention. It develops the hardware and software technologies required to run robots, autonomous vehicles, industrial systems, and more, and its revenue more than tripled year over year during the third quarter. It's now on track to generate $25 billion in total sales for the current fiscal year (which ends on Jan. 31, 2027), so it could soon become a key source of growth for the entire company. Kress also said Nvidia could deliver $130 billion in total revenue during the fourth quarter, exceeding Wall Street's consensus expectation of $125.1 billion. Plus, she told investors that revenue could grow by 75% during fiscal 2028, upping the company's original forecast of 70% from a few months ago. That was a very positive surprise, and it dispels some of the speculation that Nvidia's sales will take a major hit amid any potential investigations into its dealings with customers in Southeast Asia. Jensen Huang and Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, are expected to testify before Congress in early December, where they will be questioned about potential national security breaches involving the prohibited sale of advanced AI chips to China. It's difficult to know what will come of these hearings, but I think investors are now being compensated for the potential risks because of Nvidia's rock-bottom valuation. Nvidia stock is trading at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of just 16.2 as I write this on Nov. 19, which is a fraction of its 10-year average of 61.1. It's also the lowest valuation in a decade. Moreover, Wall Street still believes Nvidia will grow its earnings to $16.61 per share in fiscal 2028, placing its forward P/E ratio at just 9.1. For some perspective, that's less than half the forward P/E of the Nasdaq-100 index, which is 20.7, so Nvidia looks extremely undervalued compared to a collective of America's leading technology giants. As a result, I think there is room for Nvidia stock to trade significantly higher over the next 12 months, provided the company's fiscal 2028 guidance remains intact and isn't disrupted by a slowdown in AI infrastructure spending, a loss of market share, or government investigations. These are genuine risks, but Kress's decision to raise the forecast suggests the sales pipeline is robust enough to weather them. Even if Nvidia stock doubles over the next year, it will still be cheaper than the Nasdaq-100 on a P/E basis, so I feel confident predicting a price of at least $200. But I think there is a real chance the stock reclaims its previous high of $239. This theme extends beyond NVIDIA. See which of 53 AI infrastructure stocks may still merit a closer look. The shares cost US$186 at the start of the period, and Nvidia was already treated as the key AI hardware supplier that could define how much compute the world could realistically build. One bullish story saw a fair value of US$209, a rough estimate of what the stock might be worth if AI demand kept driving 26.8% revenue growth with profit margins reaching 55.7% and a future P/E of 35.2x. The more cautious view put fair value closer to US$153, assuming even faster 34.9% top-line expansion and 55.8% margins but arguing that a future P/E of 34.0x left little room for geopolitical or custom-ASIC risk. Nvidia’s Q3 2027 report showed revenue of US$115,844m and net income of US$65,287m, with net margin edging up to 56.4%. That profitability profile sat in the zone the optimistic case pictured for strong earnings power supporting a premium P/E, even as later leadership turmoil and governance concerns gave the cautious camp fresh material on key person and geopolitical risk. The useful takeaway is clear. When a story leans on rich multiples, track whether margins and absolute profit, not just sales, move toward the scenario that was assumed. As AI workloads expand, appetite for bandwidth and storage can influence how much practical computing customers actually obtain from Nvidia hardware. Wall Street is sharply divided—with analysts pointing to a clash between some of the strongest earnings growth in corporate history and one of the most severe leadership, regulatory, and market crises Silicon Valley has ever seen. Shares of Nvidia (NVDA) closed at $125.53 on Friday, November 20, 2026, plunging 14.01% on the day to extend a seven-week losing streak. Since hitting a record 52-week high of $243.37 on October 6, the AI chip giant has shed more than $2.7 trillion in market value—nearly $900 billion of it wiped out during this week’s sell-off alone. BREAKING: The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is launching an investigation into "potential accounting issues" at Nvidia.Nvidia stock, $NVDA, extends losses to over -8% on the day and -45% since October 6th. pic.twitter.com/Z1yUJrCypF While deeply oversold technicals and booming revenue forecasts suggest a near-term relief bounce is plausible, strategists warn that a sustained climb back toward record highs will not happen overnight. Nvidia’s slide is the product of an extraordinary pileup of company-specific shocks hitting at the exact moment Wall Street’s broader AI trade began to buckle: Despite the panic, several fundamental and technical factors keep a recovery—or at least a sharp bounce—firmly on the table: Bears argue that the current sell-off is not a temporary dip, but the start of a longer structural reset for both Nvidia and the AI economy: Speculation over Huang’s next act has already become a sideshow for NVDA traders. At a White House briefing Friday, President Donald Trump publicly defended Huang, saying, "I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance," and suggesting Nvidia accept his apology and reinstate him. Elon Musk and Uber founder Travis Kalanick have also backed a petition calling for Huang’s return, while Musk replied on X that hiring Huang at SpaceX "would be an honor." Huang remains Nvidia’s largest individual shareholder, holding a stake still worth roughly $102 billion at Friday’s close. title: Nvidia (NVDA) shares fell sharply as SEC investigates potential accounting issues - Beinsure
content: Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) shares fell sharply after reports that the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is investigating potential accounting issues at the AI chipmaker, adding to a series of legal and regulatory problems that have erased approximately $1 tn from its market capitalization in a week. SEC enforcement staff are examining the company’s accounting practices, Reuters reported, citing two people familiar with the confidential investigation. The Wall Street Journal had previously disclosed the existence of an SEC inquiry without identifying its focus. The investigation contributed to another sell-off on Friday, November 20. Nvidia shares fell approximately 14% during the session, extending their weekly decline to 23%, the company’s worst weekly performance since October 2008. The stock had already been under pressure following the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang and allegations involving his relationship with a woman suspected by US authorities of working for Chinese intelligence. Strong quarterly earnings reported Tuesday failed to reverse the decline. The SEC declined to comment on its investigation, while Nvidia representatives did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Neither the specific accounting matters under examination nor the date the inquiry began has been established publicly. An SEC investigation does not constitute evidence of wrongdoing and may conclude without enforcement action. The investigation has renewed attention on Nvidia’s geographic revenue reporting, particularly its treatment of sales associated with Singapore. In 2025, Nvidia changed its method for reporting revenue by geographic location, replacing customer billing addresses with customer headquarters. The company said the revised approach provided a more accurate representation of the geographical distribution of its business. The change removed Singapore as a separate category in Nvidia’s geographic revenue breakdown. The Financial Times reported that Nvidia introduced the revised methodology even as sales attributed to Singapore had increased to almost half of global revenue under the previous reporting approach. The distinction between billing locations, customer headquarters and final destinations of semiconductor products has become a concern because of US restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China. Nvidia reported $19.7 bn in revenue from customers headquartered in China during fiscal 2026. That figure does not establish whether any products were shipped or transferred in violation of US export controls. The SEC has not publicly indicated whether geographic revenue reporting is part of its investigation. Suggestions that the inquiry involves Singapore-related sales or the ultimate destination of Nvidia chips remain speculative. Nvidia is also facing scrutiny over its historical business relationship with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company previously led by Alice Huang. US authorities suspect Alice Huang of having links to Chinese intelligence, an allegation denied by China. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang acknowledged an extramarital affair in a November 8 statement following reports about his relationship with Alice Huang, although he did not identify her by name. Megaspeed has historically been a major purchaser of Nvidia processors. US authorities have investigated the company since 2024 over possible violations of semiconductor export restrictions involving alleged shipments of advanced AI chips to China. The US Justice and Commerce departments confirmed the investigations during the week. Megaspeed said Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and maintained that its business operations were lawful. Reuters has been unable to contact Alice Huang for comment. The investigations follow years of US restrictions on advanced semiconductor exports to China, introduced in 2022 over concerns that the technology could strengthen Beijing’s military capabilities. Southeast Asia has attracted particular attention because of the possibility that intermediaries could obtain restricted chips for Chinese customers. According to reports about the Megaspeed investigation, a US Commerce Department official discovered Nvidia equipment still packaged at a Malaysian data center site in 2024, raising questions about whether the hardware was intended for onward shipment. The allegations have increased political scrutiny of Nvidia’s business relationships and its compliance with US export regulations. Jensen Huang is scheduled to testify behind closed doors on December 1 before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the House Intelligence Committee. A transcript of the proceedings could subsequently be released. The SEC accounting inquiry is separate from an ongoing Justice Department examination of Nvidia’s acquisition activities and commercial practices. Reuters reported in October that the Justice Department was reviewing Nvidia’s $12.9 bn agreement to acquire open-source AI platform Hugging Face. That review forms part of a broader antitrust investigation into Nvidia’s acquisitions and business conduct. The company consequently faces several distinct areas of regulatory scrutiny, including potential accounting issues, semiconductor export controls and competition concerns. No public information establishes that these investigations concern the same conduct or will result in enforcement action. Nvidia’s financial relationships with AI companies and cloud infrastructure providers have also drawn attention from analysts and investors. Chipmakers have participated in financing arrangements that help customers purchase processors and develop data centers. Nvidia has invested in AI businesses, supported cloud providers and provided guarantees associated with infrastructure projects using its equipment. Critics argue that such arrangements can complicate assessments of revenue quality and the financial risks companies retain through their relationships with customers. One concern involves circular financing, where capital supplied to an AI company or infrastructure provider can ultimately support purchases of equipment from the investor or its business partners. These transactions are not inherently improper, but their structure and disclosure can affect investors’ understanding of commercial demand and financial exposure. SEC enforcement chief David Woodcock told in October that the regulator was reviewing corporate disclosures by AI companies to determine whether investors were receiving adequate information about potential risks. During Nvidia’s Tuesday earnings call, interim CEO and former CFO Colette Kress defended the company’s role in supporting AI industry development but said it would become substantially more selective about future financing agreements. The company has not publicly connected that policy change to the SEC investigation. The investigation comes as the SEC under President Donald Trump has shifted its enforcement priorities toward traditional securities fraud, including accounting and financial reporting violations. The agency has reduced its emphasis on some other enforcement areas while establishing a dedicated financial reporting and accounting unit within its enforcement division. The unit is intended to develop cases involving accounting practices, auditing and corporate financial disclosures. The existence of an inquiry involving Nvidia does not establish that the company misstated its financial results or violated securities laws. SEC investigators have not publicly identified any transactions, reporting periods or accounting standards under examination. The latest investigation has intensified selling pressure on Nvidia following a series of disclosures involving its former chief executive, export-control compliance and corporate transactions. The company lost more than a third of its market value during the broader crisis, with the latest weekly decline representing approximately $1 tn in lost capitalization. Nvidia’s Friday sell-off also affected the personal wealth of Jensen Huang. According to Forbes, Huang lost another $17.3 bn on November 20, reducing his estimated net worth to $110.2 bn and placing him 17th on its global billionaires ranking. His estimated fortune has declined by more than 25% since November 9, the first trading session following his public acknowledgment of the affair. The immediate question for Nvidia investors is whether the SEC’s confidential accounting inquiry develops into a formal enforcement case. The regulator has disclosed neither its specific concerns nor a timetable, leaving the investigation’s potential financial and legal consequences undetermined. title: AMD vs. Nvidia: Which AI Chip Stock Is the Better Buy on the Dip? - The Motley Fool
content: AMD and Nvidia both got hammered this month. Only one is the better bargain. By Prosper Junior Bakiny – Nov 21, 2026 at 3:30AM EST The semiconductor industry is experiencing a sell-off, and even some of the sector's leaders, including Advanced Micro Devices (AMD -13.25%) and Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%), haven't escaped the bloodbath. Both companies have faced headwinds in recent weeks and have lost significant market value as a result. AMD's shares have dropped 21% over the past month, while Nvidia's are down 40%. Which of these two stocks is a better buy right now? AMD was the subject of a short-seller report by Hunterbrook Media alleging that the semiconductor leader may have violated export restrictions, since some of its firmware ended up at a blacklisted Chinese server manufacturer. However, Hunterbrook Media itself acknowledges that it doesn't know whether AMD itself supplied the software. Meanwhile, Reuters has said it couldn't independently verify these claims, while AMD has denied them. So, this may be a giant nothingburger, after all. Yet, the stock fell because of the short-seller report, which arguably creates an attractive entry point. AMD is capitalizing on the agentic AI boom, thanks to its market-leading CPU (central processing unit) servers. Third-quarter revenue jumped 45% year over year to $13.4 billion, while data center revenue soared 97% year over year to $8.5 billion. AMD's non-GAAP earnings per share (EPS) were $2.09, up 74% compared to the year-ago period. AMD sees its revenue jump by more than 80% in 2027, while it expects its server CPU total addressable market to grow at a compound annual rate of more than 50% and reach $220 billion by 2030. That paints a very bright picture for the company's future. Nvidia is going through a transition. The company's co-founder and longtime CEO, Jensen Huang, was involved in a scandal involving extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. If you’d invested $5,000 then, you’d be sitting on $1,631,761 today.* Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. Huang stepped down as a result, a big blow to the company, given what he had built up to that point. Nvidia's board has appointed its CFO, Colette Kress, as interim CEO while it continues its search for its next leader. Despite all that mess, the company's financial results remain excellent. In the third quarter of its fiscal year 2027, which ended on Oct. 25, Nvidia's revenue increased by 103% year over year to $115.8 billion. The company's data center revenue soared 110% year over year to $107.6 billion. Nvidia's non-GAAP EPS was $2.68, up 111% year over year. Nvidia's quarterly update blew past expectations, and its guidance was impressive as well. The semiconductor leader expects $130 billion in revenue (at the midpoint) in its upcoming fourth quarter, representing an almost 91% year-over-year increase. And Nvidia expects its revenue to grow about 75% year over year in its fiscal year 2028, which will cover most of the calendar year 2027. The loss of Huang is a problem, but Nvidia has many advantages that remain intact, including technological expertise, deep relationships with many corporations it does business with, and its CUDA ecosystem, which provides a wide moat from switching costs. With the right leader at the helm, it could still beat the market over the long run. Nvidia currently generates higher revenue and profits, and is growing both metrics faster. It also boasts higher gross margins. However, Nvidia's search for a new CEO introduces significant uncertainty. AMD's short-seller-related problems aren't nearly as dire, in my view. Further, AMD's revenue growth is accelerating, particularly within its all-important data center segment, while Nvidia's revenue growth could decline next year. Does that make AMD the better buy? We'd need to look at valuation as well, and in that category, Nvidia is the winner, as seen in their respective price-to-earnings (P/E) ratios above. Nvidia might be facing tougher headwinds right now, but the market has adjusted for that by giving the company much lower valuation multiples. Nvidia is far too cheap at current levels, in my view, and while I'd also buy AMD's shares right now, Nvidia's look even more attractive. If you think you've had a bad week, just be glad you're not on Nvidia's (NASDAQ:NVDA) management team. Shares of the top AI stock fell 23% this week, wiping out roughly $1 trillion from its market cap. It was its worst weekly performance since October 2008 during the height of the financial crisis. The slide was initially sparked by Jensen Huang's resignation the week before, and even a strong earnings report on Tuesday wasn't enough to stem the sell-off. On Friday, Nvidia stock plunged 14%, heading sharply lower in the afternoon after Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission had opened an investigation into the company over accounting irregularities. That comes in addition to multiple investigations from different agencies and branches of the federal government over Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese agent and possible violation of chip export rules. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. Continue » Reuters said that the SEC was investigating Nvidia's accounting practices, but did not provide many details beyond that. Its report came three days after The Wall Street Journal said the SEC was investigating Nvidia, but did not say what for. Given the other news last week and the Commerce Dept. issuing tighter chip export rules to Southeast Asia, the SEC probe could focus on how Nvidia reports geographic revenue, which potentially obfuscates where its chips end up. Last year, it changed how it records geographic revenue, shifting it from billing addresses to customer headquarters. As a result of that change, the company no longer reports revenue from Singapore as its own line item. In fiscal 2026, Nvidia recorded $19.7 billion in revenue from customers headquartered in China, likely from permitted chips, though the SEC may be curious about how chips that ended up in China via other countries were recorded. It's important for investors to understand that an investigation doesn't mean that Nvidia committed fraud, or that it will face any enforcement actions. A probe is not evidence of wrongdoing, and many are closed without going further. Given the other news surrounding Nvidia, the SEC probe seems less surprising and may not be as impactful on the stock as it otherwise would be, as the company is already in turmoil. Even a finding of wrongdoing wouldn't be a terminal event for Nvidia, though it could damage its reputation, in addition to any fines or consequences the company could face. Executives at Super Micro Computer, a server-maker and close partner of Nvidia, were charged by the DOJ with conspiring to divert AI servers to China, though Supermicro's internal investigation found that no one on the senior management team was aware of the diversion scheme. It will take months or longer for the investigations into Nvidia to play out, and the company is likely to continue to receive scrutiny from the media in the wake of Huang's departure and the myriad investigations now surrounding it. Investors will note that Nvidia's forward P/E has fallen all the way to 8 as the stock has plunged, but with so much uncertainty surrounding the stock, buying it seems speculative at this point, and the stock's future performance depends on what the investigations uncover. Nvidia's "circular financing" is also in the spotlight after the change in leadership, and that could get attention from the SEC as well. There's simply so much we don't know about the stock and its future right now. Risk-tolerant investors may choose to buy the stock at the current price, but they should be aware that the volatility for Nvidia, after it's fallen for seven sessions in a row, is likely to continue. NVIDIA — After a 36% Drop from All-Time Highs: The Structural Factors Its New CEO Must Focus On Yesterday, Nvidia $NVDA reported extraordinary financial results for its fiscal third quarter: record revenues of $115.8 billion (up 103% year-over-year, with Data Center revenue reaching $107.6 billion) and a net income of $65.3 billion, crushing Wall Street expectations in its first earnings report under interim CEO Colette Kress. Wall Street views this—alongside a bullish $130 billion Q4 revenue outlook—as absolute proof that the revenue machine is running at full throttle. However, as Nvidia enters this new leadership chapter following the departure of Jensen Huang, the incoming CEO will have to navigate a far more fragile architectural reality: direct sales to hyperscalers (AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and Meta) account for 50% to 55% of Nvidia’s total revenue—and when you factor in the indirect sales channeled through the rest of the ecosystem, the true dependency on these cloud giants is even higher. With such heavy exposure to just a handful of hyperscalers, any strategic shift, budget cut, or architectural pivot on their part can significantly alter Nvidia’s future growth trajectory. Beyond these headline figures, the vast majority of Nvidia's ecosystem investments continue to flow directly through their infrastructure, masking deep structural vulnerabilities behind short-term demand. To explore these potential vulnerabilities in Nvidia's GPU demand, we must examine the different subsectors in which Nvidia has invested (the first step before deciding whether to invest or not is always to map out the underlying architecture and understand where we truly stand). Section 1: Subsectors Where Nvidia Is Deploying Its Capital Before breaking down Nvidia’s portfolio investments, it is critical to note a major shift already reshaping cloud demand: inference has overtaken training, now accounting for 55% to 65% of total AI cloud compute. While frontier model training required massive, densely interconnected clusters where Nvidia’s GPUs and CUDA software were indispensable—due to the raw parallel processing power needed to build models from scratch—the industry is maturing toward high-volume inference, which simply means running already-trained models to answer daily user queries at scale. This transition is about to accelerate sharply due to a new physical and regulatory bottleneck driven directly by recent U.S. midterm election outcomes. Across battleground states, voters pushed back aggressively against soaring household electricity bills and grid strain caused by massive AI data centers. Democratic candidates capitalized on this exact mandate—campaigning on strict legislative moratoria, mandatory grid impact audits, and rigorous utility permitting reviews to protect local ratepayers. When hyperscalers face strict caps and delays on how many new power-hungry data centers they can plug into the grid, they can no longer expand brute-force training capacity at will; instead, they are forced to maximize output per watt from existing infrastructure—accelerating the shift toward standardized inference where their own custom silicon (ASICs) excels. For a deeper analysis of how these electoral shifts and grid constraints are slowing down data center expansion, readers can consult my post published on November 6, 2026: Behind the Market Crash: The Real Drivers of the Massive Tech and Semiconductor Sell-Off — And Who Will Emerge as the True Winners? (November 6, 2026). With this structural shift in mind, let’s analyze the core subsectors where Nvidia has invested to uncover their underlying vulnerabilities. Subsector 1: Nvidia's investments in Neoclouds (CoreWeave, Nebius, Nscale) Nvidia backs specialized GPU cloud providers—known as "neoclouds"—with both equity and preferential chip allocations so these firms can build out AI data centers at breakneck speed. On paper, neoclouds look like a new, independent class of major hardware buyers that reduce Nvidia’s reliance on the hyperscalers. In practice, neoclouds operate primarily as overflow capacity subcontractors for the hyperscalers themselves—for instance, Microsoft has relied heavily on multi-billion-dollar contracts with CoreWeave to bridge its own short-term data center bottlenecks. The Result: This segment represents fragile, cyclical demand for Nvidia. Neoclouds do not control the end-enterprise customer relationship, and their business model depends on hyperscalers facing temporary capacity shortages. As AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud finish building their own data centers, those hyperscalers have every financial incentive to pull those workloads back in-house rather than pay a middleman markup—leaving neocloud utilization, and their future GPU orders, highly vulnerable. Vulnerability for Nvidia: High. Neoclouds rely on debt-financed expansion and temporary capacity bottlenecks at the hyperscalers. While skeptics might argue that hyperscalers will simply buy the GPUs that neoclouds stop ordering once workloads move in-house, that transfer is not a one-for-one replacement: as workloads shift from model training to inference, Nvidia's GPUs will become less necessary because hyperscalers will rely more on their own custom chips for these models. For more details on this subsector, readers can consult my post published on October 23: Inside the Neocloud Trap: What CoreWeave, Nebius, and the AI Gold Rush Are Hiding (October 23). Subsector 2: Nvidia's investments in Foundation Model Labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Mistral) Nvidia invests billions of dollars directly into AI model labs—such as OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, and Mistral—so that these companies use that capital to buy or rent Nvidia GPUs. On the surface, this makes Wall Street believe that demand for Nvidia’s chips is diversifying beyond the hyperscalers. The reality, however, is that these AI labs do not own hyperscale data centers. When OpenAI, Anthropic, or Mistral receive that cash from Nvidia and venture backers, they turn around and spend it on massive multi-year cloud commitments with the hyperscalers (Azure, AWS, and Google Cloud) to rent the compute capacity needed to train and run their models. The Result: Even though these AI labs route their capital through the hyperscalers' infrastructure, Nvidia’s position in frontier model training remains resilient for now due to deep developer entrenchment in the CUDA software ecosystem and superior NVLink interconnect speeds. However, as the broader AI market shifts away from heavy model training and toward high-volume, cost-sensitive inference, the nature of demand changes entirely. In this new phase, hyperscalers no longer depend on Nvidia's training moats; instead, hyperscalers are aggressively deploying their own custom ASICs (such as Google’s TPUs and Amazon’s Trainium) to handle standardized inference workloads in-house, bypassing Nvidia entirely and destroying future GPU demand. Vulnerability for Nvidia: Low in Training / High in Inference Transition. While frontier model training remains anchored to Nvidia hardware due to high technical friction and CUDA lock-in, the industry's inevitable maturation toward scaled inference strips away that protection. As workloads shift away from training, hyperscalers hold all the leverage to route traffic through their own cost-efficient silicon—directly cannibalizing Nvidia's future revenue growth. Subsector 3: Nvidia's investments in AI Software & Vertical Applications (Perplexity AI, Harvey, SoundHound) Nvidia deploys venture capital into AI software startups and vertical applications—such as Perplexity AI in conversational search, Harvey in legal AI, and SoundHound in voice AI—to stimulate end-market adoption of artificial intelligence. Unlike cloud providers, however, these software companies do not buy physical GPUs from Nvidia or build their own data centers. Instead, they use their venture funding to rent cloud compute and API capacity directly from the hyperscalers (AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud) to run their applications for end users. The Result: This layer generates strictly indirect demand that funnels straight back into the hyperscalers' infrastructure, concentrating buying power in the exact same three or four cloud giants. Furthermore, while training is protected by CUDA, enterprise and consumer software applications generate primarily high-volume inference workloads—answering user queries in real time rather than training models from scratch. Because software-level abstraction removes CUDA lock-in at the application layer, hyperscalers can steadily migrate this inference traffic onto their own lower-cost custom ASICs without disrupting the end user—gradually eroding Nvidia’s share of incremental compute growth. Vulnerability for Nvidia: Moderate. While seeding software applications successfully expands overall AI compute demand, these workloads consist predominantly of standardized inference rather than complex model training. As workloads shift from model training to inference, Nvidia's GPUs will become less necessary because hyperscalers will rely more on their own custom chips for these models. Subsector 4: Nvidia's investments in Autonomous Vehicles, Robotics & Physical AI (Figure AI, Serve Robotics, Wayve, WeRide) Nvidia also deploys capital into autonomous vehicles, humanoid robotics, and "Physical AI" startups—such as Figure AI, Serve Robotics, Wayve, and WeRide—to establish its hardware and software stack as the foundational operating system for machines operating in the physical world. Unlike cloud software or foundation model labs, these companies do not rely on hyperscaler data centers to execute their core workloads; instead, they require real-time, low-latency onboard inference directly at the edge (powered by Nvidia DRIVE and Jetson chips) alongside physics-accurate digital twin simulations (via Nvidia Omniverse and Isaac). The Result: This is one of the few ecosystem segments where demand does not funnel back through AWS, Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud. While Alphabet and Amazon operate closed, proprietary robotaxi subsidiaries (Waymo and Zoox, respectively), neither they nor Microsoft or Meta commercialize horizontal edge-computing chips or physical simulation platforms for third-party automakers and robotics developers. Consequently, hyperscalers cannot cannibalize this workload with their cloud-centric custom ASICs, allowing Nvidia to capture an end-to-end moat—from simulation training in the lab to embedded inference inside the vehicle or robot itself. Vulnerability for Nvidia: Low to Moderate. Nvidia maintains a genuine architectural advantage here because hyperscalers do not compete as B2B silicon suppliers at the physical edge. The vulnerability is only moderate insofar as commercial adoption timelines for autonomous fleets and humanoid robotics remain multi-year capital cycles that are still too small today to offset a near-term slowdown in massive data center GPU orders. Section 2: Do Nvidia's Investments in These Subsectors Actually Impact Its Bottom Line? Wall Street loves to treat Nvidia's web of minority equity stakes across neoclouds, model labs, and software startups as proof of a self-sustaining, diversified ecosystem. A basic financial reality check shows why this narrative falls apart. The investments that Nvidia holds in these subsectors experience valuation shifts. Under U.S. accounting rules (ASC 321), any appreciation or depreciation in those stakes is included directly in Nvidia’s Income Statement, meaning they have a direct impact on its net income. However, looking at the numbers as of September 2026, that "other income, net" account was barely 8.7% of total revenues during the first nine months of the year. While these paper gains pad the bottom line, they pale in comparison to Nvidia's massive core hardware revenues. More importantly, the incoming CEO will need to closely monitor the vulnerable subsectors we outlined above. If growth in those fragile segments decelerates, it won't just trigger negative valuation adjustments flowing into the income statement—it will serve as the canary in the coal mine. A slowdown among those startups means their hardware purchases are drying up, exposing the core risk: many of these companies only bought Nvidia GPUs in the first place because Nvidia injected the capital right back into them. The sole objective of this post is neither to be bullish nor bearish, but rather to analyze Nvidia's architecture and core ecosystem sectors to understand where we currently stand and what underlying trends are emerging. Looking at what we have examined, it is critical to assess whether the company's massive past growth will be sustainable over the next 5 to 10 years. Going forward, it is essential to monitor how the interim CEO—and whoever follows—addresses Nvidia's vulnerable points while adapting the business to the rising dominance of inference models and a slower-growth data center environment shaped by the implementation of the new legislative agenda following recent elections. From a personal capital allocation standpoint, I am not initiating a new position just yet—I still need to see how the new leadership executes its strategy to sustain the business through these structural shifts. Naturally, if I had bought my shares two or three years ago, I would sit on enough margin of safety to comfortably hold through this transition. Notably, according to TIKR Terminal, Nvidia is currently trading at its lowest EV/EBIT multiple in five years. A week ago, the idea of Nvidia $NVDA operating without Jensen Huang was almost inconceivable. But it just happened. Bloomberg is reporting that the only CEO Nvidia has ever had just resigned amid a scandal involving two extramarital affairs. On Sunday, Nvidia’s founder and CEO sent employees a memo admitting he’d been unfaithful to his wife of more than 40 years. The affair was reportedly with Alice Huang (no relation), a Chinese national who was based in Singapore (but is now reportedly back in Beijing) and ran a company that bought billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips in 2024 and 2025. US intelligence officials reportedly believe she’s a Chinese spy who targeted Jensen for nefarious purposes. Nvidia’s board launched an investigation the same day while saying it had full confidence in Jensen. The stock lost about $430 billion of value on Monday and Tuesday. On Wednesday it bounced back almost 3%. Then, Wednesday evening, The Wall Street Journal reported that the board is preparing to oust him. The Journal and The New York Times also reported a second affair, this one with a senior Nvidia executive who runs the company’s healthcare business. Bloomberg reports the board has hired an outside firm to find replacement candidates and is weighing a temporary CEO while it searches. The board met last night (Wednesday). Nvidia fell 8% to 9% in after-hours trading. If that holds, Nvidia will have lost about $600 billion of market value since Sunday. Then, just this morning, Bloomberg reported that Jensen Huang resigned. I want to explain what’s happened, why the board’s math changed overnight, and why Jensen matters so much to this company. Then I’ll talk about what it means for the business. Confirmed: Jensen admitted an affair in Sunday’s memo. “There is no excuse for what I did,” he wrote. He didn’t name the woman. Also confirmed: Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation, run by a committee of independent directors. It hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz and former federal prosecutor Joon Kim. Before Sunday, Nvidia had described Jensen’s dealings with Alice Huang as normal business between a supplier and a customer’s executive. Jensen himself told Bloomberg last month that it was all “completely normal and not unusual.” Reported but not confirmed by Nvidia: That US intelligence concluded Alice Huang was working for China’s main spy agency. That her company, Megaspeed, may have helped move Nvidia chips into China. That Jensen had a second affair with a senior Nvidia executive. That the board is preparing to remove him. That it’s working with a search firm and considering a temporary CEO. China’s government calls the spy allegations a smear. It’s not going to admit anything, obviously. Megaspeed denies any wrongdoing. Nobody has been charged with anything. And as I write, Nvidia hasn’t commented on the board meeting. Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work. Earlier this week, I would have told you the odds of the board firing Jensen were low. Here’s why… and why that’s no longer true. CEO scandals get a ton of attention, but they rarely cost CEOs their jobs. One firm that tracks CEO departures found that of nearly 3,000 CEO exits at Russell 3000 companies since January 2017, just 1.6% happened amid misconduct allegations. When boards do act, it’s almost never because of the affair itself. It’s because the CEO broke company rules or hid something from the board. McDonald’s fired Steve Easterbrook in 2019 over a relationship with an employee. It later recovered more than $100 million after accusing him of lying about other relationships. BP’s Bernard Looney resigned in 2023 after admitting he hadn’t been fully transparent with the board. Nestlé pushed out its CEO last year for failing to disclose a relationship with someone who reported to him. The pattern: A relationship with an employee and a failure to disclose are the triggers that push boards to act. Through Tuesday, the Jensen story didn’t fit that pattern. It was an affair with a customer’s top executive, who was allegedly acting in the interest of the Chinese Communist Party. That raised national security concerns and a possible conflict of interest, but the facts were still being investigated. A reported affair with a senior executive inside Nvidia is a different animal. Workplace relationships between a CEO and a subordinate in the company are the textbook case where boards say the rules leave them no choice. Add the company’s earlier insistence that the Alice Huang relationship was ordinary business, and you can see why the board’s math changed in one night. There’s the political side, too. Nvidia’s board was already under fire. It has no chairman. Several directors have served for decades. The law firm James Drury Partners ranked Nvidia’s corporate governance 609th among more than 650 big US companies. Plus, the board said it had “no reason to believe” anything was compromised before its own investigation even started. That guts its credibility. Directors who’ve been criticized for deferring to a founder (whether deserved or not) now have every reason to show they won’t. That’s my read, not something they’ve said. But I’d bet that was being discussed before Jensen made the decision for the board. All of this sits on top of a national security story that hasn’t gone away. Nvidia’s best chips are the closest thing the US has to a strategic weapon in the AI race. That’s why the US bans exporting the most advanced ones to China. Jensen has been one of the president’s most trusted AI advisers, and he’s lobbied hard to loosen those rules. Doing that while in a close relationship with someone US officials believe reported to Chinese intelligence is a counterintelligence nightmare, even if nothing was ever compromised. The Justice Department is reportedly leading several investigations involving Alice Huang. House committees asked Jensen to brief them in private on November 18. That’s the same day Trump is scheduled to meet Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, where chip access is one of the hottest topics. Meanwhile, Congress is weighing tougher chip export rules in the big annual defense bill. Whatever the board might have decided, that pressure isn’t going away anytime soon. To really get why this matters so much for investors, we need to talk about how unusual Jensen’s role is. “Key-man risk” is a simple idea. A company depends so heavily on one person that losing them would seriously hurt the business. In my opinion, aside from the companies run by Elon Musk, Nvidia has more of it than any company in the world. Washington and the Market: Examining the Gridlock Myth A blue tsunami swept Congress, governors' offices, and statehouses across the nation earlier this month, mainly due to dissatisfaction with inflation and the war in Iran but also on concern that new data centers are being rubber-stamped with minimal citizen input. The Democratic majority in Congress is ready to take aim at artificial intelligence (AI) data centers beginning in January 2027. Dominance of the presidency, Senate, and House by one party matters a great deal in terms of the ability to set the legislative agenda while avoiding the presidential veto. Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025 with the GOP in charge of the Senate and House of Representatives, albeit with slim majorities. That allowed the president's party to set high tariffs, engage in aggressive immigration enforcement, and even start a foreign war with little pushback from Congress. The popular Wall Street wisdom is that the best outcome in Washington is gridlock. Investors perceive that when one party has hegemony, which we define as controlling the presidency, House, and Senate simultaneously, ideology supplants pragmatism and compromise, expensive and impractical legislation is passed, and the market suffers the consequences. That hegemony is now gone, and the next two years in Washington could be very different from the first two. Our analysis of S&P 500 performance since 1945 does not substantiate the widely held perception that 'gridlock is best,' however. Our work suggests that stock market performance as measured by the S&P 500 in years in which one party has hegemony is little different than its performance in years in which neither party has complete control. Recent history is instructive - and also cautionary. One such year of hegemony was 2017, when the GOP controlled the presidency, House, and Senate and the S&P 500 delivered capital appreciation exceeding 19%. Then came 2018. In a year in which the GOP retained its hegemony across the presidency, House and Senate, the S&P 500 declined by more than 6%. Joe Biden never enjoyed hegemony, yet the market roared in his first year (up 27%) only to collapse in his second year (down 19%). Investors should not assume a statistical tendency constitutes a performance guarantee. We believe the market drivers in any year have more to do with the economy, earnings, employment, and inflation than with the various occupants of the White House and Congress. Still, it is worth examining how the market fares under multiple Washington scenarios. In a statistical nutshell, the S&P 500 since 1945 has done very well when one party held hegemony across the presidency, House, and Senate. And the stock market does best on average when one's party's standard-bearer is president. Read on to find out which party is which. Washington by the Numbers Please note that as a starting point to our analysis, we analyzed market performance by the years in which the president and Congress actually served, not the election year. Thus, for the Eisenhower years, we begin with 1953, when Ike took office, not 1952, when he was elected. And our analysis includes only complete (four-year) presidencies, so we have not included 2025 and 2026. In our market analysis below, we look at all the years from 1945 to 2024. But we also consider the two distinct periods of 1945-80 and 1981-2024. Our choice of 1981 as a dividing line is not arbitrary. The successful conclusion of World War II ushered in what is seen as a golden era in the U.S. Beginning in 1945, our enemies (also our chief economic competitors) were prostrate, the government provided for the indigent for the first time in history, and the massive suburban migration fueled an enormous housing and infrastructure boom. Regionally, the South had not yet repudiated the Democratic Party, and the white ethnic working class of the Northeast was also solidly Democratic. As a result, for most of the period from 1945 to 1980, the Democratic party either enjoyed true hegemony or controlled at least two of the three levers of power. The Democrats enjoyed true hegemony for 18 years from 1945 to 1980. The years since 1981 have been a different story for FDR's party. Democrats have experienced hegemony for just four years since 1981. These were the first two years for President Bill Clinton and the first two years for President Barack Obama. President Clinton tried and failed to pass a national healthcare plan. President Obama used that brief period of hegemony (2009-10) to push through the initiative - the Affordable Care Act (ACA) - that will likely define his presidency. The Reagan years heralded the abandonment of the Democratic party by its historical bedrock voters in the Northeast and South. The Reagan years also coincided with the expansion of the Treasury market and the demise of the traditional defined benefit pension plan, two events with major consequences for investing patterns. Perhaps because old alignments were still in flux in the 1980s, hugely popular President Ronald Reagan never enjoyed true hegemony. The GOP has experienced 3-0 hegemony for just eight years since 1945, all of them coming since 2000 (and, as noted, not including 2025-26 in our analysis). The Republican party enjoyed a four-year period of hegemony in the middle of the George W. Bush administration (2003-06). President Bush used his hegemony to pursue the increasingly unpopular war in Iraq. The GOP enjoyed a similar span in the first two years of the first Trump presidency (2017-18). President Trump used that period to push through the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act but failed to eliminate the ACA. In his second term, President Trump has used hegemony to advance his tariff, immigration, and military agendas. Washington & Wall Street by the Numbers From 1945 to 2024, the S&P 500 averaged a simple arithmetic gain of 8.8%. This tally does not include dividends; including dividends, the average annual change in the S&P 500 since 1945 is closer to 10%. Compared with today, the S&P 500 before 1980 had relatively low index values, but the change in any given year tended to be wide. On a capital appreciation basis, the S&P 500 did better from 1981 to 2024 (up 10.2% on average) than from 1945 to 1980 (up 7.1% on average). Over the 1945-2024 span, encompassing 80 years, our analysis shows 30 years in which one party controlled the Presidency, the House, and the Senate. For these 30 years, the average change in the S&P 500 (excluding dividends) was 8.9%. We also count 50 years of nonhegemony, meaning either the Democrats or Republicans controlled two of the three. For these 50 years, the average change in the S&P 500 (excluding dividends) was 8.8%. Given the skimpy 10-basis-points outperformance in years in which one party was dominant (3-0), party hegemony has not stood in the way of the stock market. And gridlock is not all it's cracked up to be in terms of investment performance. How does the market perform in years in which each of the two parties enjoys hegemony? Since 1945, the Democrats have enjoyed 22 years in which they controlled the presidency, House, and Senate; on average, the S&P 500 appreciated 7.2% in those years. The Republicans have experienced eight years in which they controlled the presidency, House, and Senate; on average, the S&P 500 appreciated 10.8% in those years. How does the market perform in years in which each of the two parties has an advantage (2-1) but neither holds hegemony? Of the 50 such years since 1945, Democrats have enjoyed a 2-1 advantage for 28 years and Republicans for 22 years. For years in which Democrats had a 2-1 advantage, the average change in the S&P 500 was 6.0%, excluding dividends. For years in which Republicans had a 2-1 advantage, the average change in the S&P 500 was 12.1%, excluding dividends. Keep in mind that the Democrats were more powerful in the post-WWII, pre-Reagan years, when market returns were lower, and Republicans have been more powerful in the years since, when returns have been generally higher. But timing does not fully explain the performance differential. Since 1945, the market appears to do better when the GOP is in charge compared to when the Democrats are in charge. But does the same hold true regarding the ultimate seat of power, the U.S. presidency? The division between the two parties on presidential leadership since 1945 is remarkably even as measured in years, but not in stock performance. For the 80 years from 1945 and 2024, the GOP has held the White House for 40 years and Democrats have held the White House for 40 years. For the 40 years since 1945 in which Democrats have held the White House, the S&P 500 has averaged appreciation of 10.6%, excluding dividends. For the 40 years since 1945 in which Republicans have held the White House, the S&P 500 has averaged appreciation of 7.0%, excluding dividends. Given that we are in a two-party system, that the market does better when the GOP is dominant (2-1) but not in hegemony (3-0), and that the market does better with Democratic presidents than with Republican presidents, the ideal stock-market scenario would appear to be periods in which the GOP controls the House and Senate and a Democrat is in the White House. Beginning in January 2027, the opposite scenario will be in place. Conclusion Each election cycle has its own nuances, and analysis of historical events gets you only so far in seeking to forecast market patterns. We would also caution that, notwithstanding the elevated sense of self-importance emanating from inside the Beltway, Washington likely ranks fairly low on the list of market drivers for any year or cycle. We have been through a somewhat uncommon period in which the prevailing market driver of recent years - AI as an economic and market force - is an area of intense interest and intervention by the president. Still, we believe this analysis supports the view that Washington gridlock is overrated as a stock market driver and that single-party dominance is not the bane to market returns it's popularly assumed to be. The company said its 10-Q, the detailed quarterly filing, would come "in the coming weeks" instead of the same evening as usual, and the release mentioned an ongoing investigation by an independent board committee. Nvidia booked about $104 billion of revenue through its Singapore unit in 2025, roughly half its sales, the Financial Times reported. The Journal said the disclosure questions include Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer US officials suspect of rerouting its chips to China. Nvidia's customers are also taking longer to pay, with bills outstanding at 64 days of sales, the most since 2022. It's not clear which of these, if any, the SEC is focused on. Washington wants answers fast. "I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday, after Jensen Huang's exit as CEO. President Trump said Friday he "would love to see Jensen be given a second chance," while criticizing the chipmaker's new leadership. California is digging in too. Attorney General Rob Bonta subpoenaed Nvidia Thursday, investigating whether its advanced chips reached China and whether the company misled investors. "Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said. The sell-off spread across chip stocks, which had their worst week since 2001, and the broader market. Baird's Ted Mortonson, a technology desk sector strategist, saw more scrutiny coming even before Friday's report. "Every single deal that Nvidia has done on circular finance is going to be put under the microscope," he said on Yahoo Finance's live show Thursday. title: Does Huang’s Exit Sink Nvidia Stock? History Is Split - Trefis
content: Today’s big story: Will 2027 Be A 2022 Repeat For Stocks? Nvidia’s board said on Tuesday’s earnings call that it does not intend to bring back Jensen Huang as CEO. Huang, the company’s co-founder, resigned with immediate effect on Nov 12. Most readers want to know who can run Nvidia without him. This article asks a different question. What happened to stocks when a founder left a market leader? The record gives no single answer. Our price data covers three founder-CEO exits at market leaders. A year later, Microsoft was down 48.0%. Apple was up 76.1%. Amazon was down 10.5%. Only Apple beat SPY, a fund that tracks the S&P 500, over one year and over three years. Here is how Nvidia has traded since the news. Nvidia fell 16.0% from the Nov 11 close to the Nov 19 close. The Nov 11 close was the last one before Huang resigned. Over the same days, Broadcom rose 0.4%. SPY fell 5.8%. On Nov 12, the day of the announcement, Nvidia fell 4.3%. Advanced Micro Devices rose 5.9% that day. Broadcom rose 5.5%. On day one, money left Nvidia while two other big chip makers rose. The board’s statement came on the evening of Tuesday, Nov 17. The results release went out at 4:20 pm, after the close. From the Nov 17 close to the Nov 19 close, Nvidia fell another 6.1%. Broadcom rose 1.5%. AMD fell 2.8%, and SPY fell 2.3%. Nvidia is down 16.0% since the last close before Huang resigned, and 6.1% since the board said he would not return. If Nvidia is a big part of your savings, a drop like that is hard to sit through without wanting to sell. The Trefis Income Solution fell less than the S&P 500 in each of the 9 big sell-offs since 2018, and it pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500’s. See how it held up. One way to check is operating margin. That is the share of each dollar of sales left after the costs of running the business. The table below shows each founder exit, the stock’s return against SPY, and the margin before and after. Source: Intrinio split-adjusted closing prices and Morningstar income statements. Returns are price only. They run from the last close before the news to the close 252 trading sessions (one year) and 756 sessions (three years) later. SPY is measured over the same sessions. Margins compare the last full fiscal year before the exit with the third full fiscal year after it. Microsoft’s margin fell from 50.9% to 41.1%. Its stock lost 51.4% over three years. Apple’s margin went from 28.2% to 28.7%. Its stock rose 87.2% over three years. Amazon breaks the pattern. Its margin rose from 5.9% to 10.8%. Yet its stock trailed SPY over one year and over three years. Three cases are too few to make a rule. We read them as examples, not odds. Nvidia’s case also differs from all three. Bill Gates handed the job to Steve Ballmer and stayed on as chairman. Steve Jobs became Apple’s chairman when he gave up the CEO job. Jeff Bezos said ahead of time that he would step down, and he stayed on as executive chair. Huang left with immediate effect and also left the board. The chief financial officer agreed to serve as interim CEO. Nvidia’s operating margin was 66.9% in the quarter to Oct 25, 2026. That was the last full quarter before Huang left. Revenue was $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier. The company’s guidance for its fourth quarter implies a GAAP operating margin of about 63.0%. That would be lower than the third quarter. In their latest reported quarters, AMD’s margin was 21.2% and Broadcom’s was 54.3%. We think the margin is the better test of Nvidia after Huang, though it is not a sure one. At Microsoft, the founder’s exit came with a falling margin. At Apple, the margin held. At Amazon, the margin rose, but the stock still trailed SPY. For the earnings case, see Why Huang’s Exit May Not Sink Nvidia Stock. Nvidia was already 27.4% below its Oct 6 record close before Huang resigned. At Thursday’s close, it was 39.0% below that record. Much of the fall came before the CEO news. The wider market also fell. SPY fell 2.0% on Thursday, Nov 19. AMD fell 11.5% from the Nov 11 close to the Nov 19 close. No company statement or filing says how much of Nvidia’s fall is about Huang. We cannot split it from the wider market’s fall. Nvidia has been this far below a high before. After first closing a third below its Nov 2021 high, it fell another 49.7% to a low in Oct 2022. It closed back at its Nov 2021 high on May 25, 2023. That was a different time, and past falls do not set the path of this one. This question is part of our coverage of the AI story. Our read: a founder leaving has not decided where a market leader’s stock went. We would watch whether Nvidia’s margin holds up. Until it settles, owners may face more drops like this week’s. Those drops are easier to sit through when the rest of your money falls less than the market does. Holding on is easier when your portfolio falls less than the market. title: Prediction: Nvidia Will Hit a New All-Time High in 2027 (Hint: Watch This Metric) - The Motley Fool
content: Nvidia has lost nearly 37% of its market value in recent weeks, but an epic recovery could be in store next year. It's been a turbulent November for Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%) as the company deals with the unexpected resignation of founder and longtime CEO Jensen Huang. Uncertainty surrounding the company's leadership transition, investigations involving ties to China, and questions about its artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure partnerships are weighing heavily on investor sentiment. Nevertheless, Nvidia's latest financial results suggest the company's business is expanding at a record pace. During its fiscal third quarter (ended Oct. 25), Nvidia generated $115.8 billion in revenue, representing 103% year-over-year growth. Meanwhile, adjusted earnings per share (EPS) climbed 111% to $2.68. Despite this impressive performance, Nvidia stock is trading roughly 37% below its all-time high. With that said, one financial metric could ultimately drive the stock to new highs: earnings per share (EPS). Nvidia has two opportunities to expand EPS over the coming year, combining organic profit growth with an enormous share repurchase program. Nvidia's first opportunity to increase EPS comes directly from its underlying business. The company is a key beneficiary of AI-driven demand from hyperscalers expanding their data center build-outs. Nvidia's data center division generated $107.6 billion in revenue during the third quarter, increasing 110% year over year. What's particularly impressive is Nvidia's ability to convert its top-line growth into substantial profits. During the third quarter, the company reported a gross margin of 74.8%. This reflects the pricing power associated with Nvidia's GPUs, networking products, and CUDA software ecosystem. These economics allow Nvidia to generate enormous profits alongside an accelerating revenue base. Although management expects gross margin to moderate to between 71% and 72% in the fourth quarter, it anticipates a recovery to between 72% and 73% in fiscal 2028. More importantly, interim CEO Colette Kress raised the company's fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook to approximately 75% year over year, up from its previous projection of 70%. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. If you’d invested $5,000 then, you’d be sitting on $1,631,761 today.* Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. Even if gross margin remains below its peak, Nvidia can still produce higher earnings through increased sales volumes and operating leverage. In other words, as revenue grows, certain operating expenses may increase at a slower rate relative to sales. This would allow additional revenue to contribute disproportionately to operating profits. The idea here is that Nvidia doesn't necessarily need to maintain record gross margins to achieve record earnings. Nvidia's second earnings catalyst is its share repurchase authorization. In September, Nvidia's board of directors approved a $150 billion increase to its existing repurchase program. As of the end of the fiscal third quarter, Nvidia had $227.3 billion remaining under its authorization. Management affirmed its intention to execute the remaining portion of the repurchase authorization by the end of fiscal 2028. This makes stock buybacks an important, albeit underrated, component of Nvidia's capital allocation strategy. The significance of Nvidia's share repurchases becomes clearer once you understand how EPS is calculated. Earnings per share equals a company's net income divided by its shares outstanding. When Nvidia repurchases and retires shares, the company effectively reduces the denominator in that equation. This means EPS can increase even if net income remains unchanged. For example, suppose a company generates $100 billion in annual net income across 25 billion shares. That would translate into EPS of $4.00. If the same company reduced its share count by 5%, while net income remained unchanged, EPS would increase to $4.21 without any additional revenue or profit growth. Stock prices are influenced by two interconnected variables: earnings per share and the valuation multiple investors are willing to pay for those earnings. A company's share price can rise even when its price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio remains unchanged, provided EPS increases. This unique relationship makes the mechanics around Nvidia's potential earnings expansion particularly interesting. Nvidia's combination of projected revenue growth, compounding profitability, and aggressive share repurchases creates a compelling outlook around next year's EPS. These catalysts provide the foundation for a bounceback in Nvidia stock even without assuming a dramatic increase in the company's valuation multiple. I think Nvidia stock could soar next year, driven by accelerating EPS growth rather than speculative enthusiasm. Against this backdrop, investors should monitor Nvidia's net income growth and changes in shares outstanding over the coming quarters. Taken together, these metrics could reveal whether Nvidia's financial performance is strong enough to overcome its recent challenges and propel the stock to new highs. title: Is Nvidia Stock a Once-in-a-Decade Buying Opportunity After Its Latest Earnings? - The Motley Fool
content: There is a light at the end of the tunnel for Nvidia. By Prosper Junior Bakiny – Nov 19, 2026 at 4:15PM EST The past week has been hard on Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%). The semiconductor leader had to separate from its co-founder and now-former CEO, Jensen Huang, after he was embroiled in a scandal involving alleged extramarital affairs, including with a woman believed to be a Chinese intelligence asset. Colette Kress, who remains CFO, has stepped up as interim CEO, leading the company through its first quarterly update since Huang's departure. And what an update it was. Nvidia once again crushed expectations, but that wasn't enough to jolt the stock, which remains down significantly since it reached a new all-time high in early October. Is Nvidia a generational buying opportunity at current levels? Death, taxes, and Nvidia's financial results coming in above analysts' projections seem to be the only certain things these days. In the third quarter of its fiscal year 2027, which ended on Oct. 25, the company's revenue came in at $115.8 billion, up 103% compared to the year-ago period. Data center revenue grew 110% year over year to $107.6 billion. Nvidia's non-GAAP gross margin was 74.9%, compared to the 73.5% reported in the prior-year quarter. The semiconductor specialist's non-GAAP operating income was $77.9 billion, rising 116% year over year, while its non-GAAP earnings per share were $2.68, up 111% year over year. The fact that profits are growing faster than revenue is a strong sign for Nvidia, given the industry's increasing competitiveness. While some investors worry that competition from custom AI chips will erode the company's pricing power in the GPU (graphics processing unit) market, as hyperscalers and other corporations increasingly opt for these custom chips, it seems, at least, that this hasn't happened yet. Improving margins are a sign that Nvidia maintains strong pricing power. Meanwhile, Nvidia's free cash flow for the period was $43.8 billion, rising 98% year over year. The company also posted excellent guidance. Nvidia expects $130 billion in revenue (at the midpoint) for its fourth quarter. That would represent a 91% year-over-year increase. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. Of course, Nvidia's financial results and guidance were only part of the story. The market wants to know how the company's efforts to replace Huang are going. Nvidia said it isn't interested in bringing back Huang, despite many people, both inside and outside the company, calling for his reinstatement. And it is actively looking for a replacement, although nobody knows when Nvidia will find someone to step into the CEO role permanently. In my opinion, that's both good and bad. It's bad because the longer this search drags on, the more uncertainty it could add to the company's prospects. But it's good because replacing a CEO as effective as Huang isn't an easy task, and the company's board is rightfully taking the time it needs to do so, or so it seems. In the meantime, several factors highlight just how massive an opportunity Nvidia could still tap into, even as it faces a more stringent regulatory environment. During the recent U.S. midterm elections, voters elected many lawmakers and politicians across various states who had promised to be stricter on the AI industry. The company raised its guidance for the fiscal year 2028, which covers most of the calendar year 2027. The company now expects revenue to grow 75% in fiscal year 2028, up from its previous projection of 70% -- and that's after also raising its guidance for its current fiscal year. If we assume Nvidia's fourth-quarter revenue lands at the midpoint, it could generate $423.7 billion this fiscal year and $741.4 billion next year, based on its projected 75% growth rate. So, given its current market cap of $3.8 trillion, Nvidia is trading at 5.1x estimated fiscal year 2028 revenue -- that's more than fair for a company growing as fast as it is, in my view. However, the CEO search does introduce some uncertainty. And we still have to account for the risk of margin erosion as industry competition intensifies. So, what's the verdict?
